Vinyl liner bid calculator

How much to charge to replace a pool liner

A published “$2,999 for a 16×32” special prices the water. A residential vinyl liner is not the water. It is wall vinyl that does not scale with square feet, a hopper the coupon never counted, stairs that wrinkle, and often a new bead track. Matching the coupon on an 18×36 hopper oval is how a sold job becomes a two-day loss after the first wrinkle in the deep end.

Open the free bid calculator

The number a water-surface special cannot see

Take a 16×32 rectangle hopper, 20 mil solid, standard bead, no stairs. That is 96 lineal feet of wall and about 961 square feet of liner — on a 512 square-foot floor. The coupon says $2,999. Raise the same shop to an 18×36 oval with wedding-cake stairs and a patterned 27-mil sheet. The water is still “about an 18×36,” so the coupon barely moves. The liner did not scale that way: more wall, hopper extra, 85 extra square feet of stairs, and 14% pattern waste the 16×32 never had.

Put a new bead track on that oval. Track is lineal feet, not water surface. Overlap bead is coping work. Over-the-fence access is not “the same job plus a ladder.”

How to price it

  1. Measure length and width. Rectangle is the product. Oval is the ellipse.
  2. Count wall vinyl: perimeter times wall height (usually 42 inches). Add hopper extra. Add stairs. That sum is liner square feet.
  3. Order square feet is liner times one plus waste. Patterned prints waste more.
  4. Price mil (20 / 27 / 30), bead, track, cove, foam, a cover, pump-down, access, and the permit allowance.
  5. Load the wage, add materials and mobilization, mark overhead on direct cost, then divide by one minus the target margin. The walk-away price is total cost.

The vinyl liner bid calculator does that arithmetic in the browser from your own hours and invoices. Starting mil rates, waste percents, and material rates are ballpark figures to replace, not a mill quote or a code table.

What this is not

This is not a building-code opinion, a permit, a construction specification, a manufacturer warranty, or an engineering stamp. Confirm the jurisdiction, the bead receiver, and a qualified professional before sending a price. The output is arithmetic on the numbers you typed.

No warranty. This free article and calculator are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from their use.

Common questions

How much to charge to replace a pool liner?

Start from the water surface, count the liner square feet a water-surface special cannot see, then add hopper extra, stairs, bead work, track, extras, and the permit. A published $2,999 special only sees length times width.

Why do walls and stairs change the price?

A 16-by-32 rectangle is 96 lineal feet of wall and about 961 square feet of liner on a 512 square-foot floor. An 18-by-36 oval with a hopper and wedding-cake stairs adds vinyl and wrinkle time the 16-by-32 coupon never priced. Matching the coupon is how the oval loses money.

Is this a building-code calculation?

No. Mil rates, waste percents, and hours here are common starting points on residential bids. They are not a building-code opinion, a permit, a manufacturer warranty, or an engineering stamp.

    Common questions

    Why does this price liner square feet instead of water surface area?

    A published “$8/sf of water” special counts only the floor's footprint, but vinyl is sold and stretched over floor plus walls plus any hopper extra plus stairs — a hopper deep-end box or a set of wedding-cake stairs adds real liner square feet the water-surface number never sees. That's why the same water surface area can price very differently depending on depth style and stairs.

    Why does an overlap or uni-bead conversion cost more than a standard bead replacement?

    Standard bead / J-hook reuses the existing track, but overlap (coping-over, no track) and uni-bead/Fast-Bead conversions change how the liner attaches at the top and often require extra prep or hardware the direct swap doesn't need. Pick the bead type that matches what's actually at your pool's coping, not just the cheapest option, since the wrong choice can mean redoing the top edge.

    Does a thicker mil liner (27 or 30) actually need more labor, or just cost more material?

    Both — a heavier liner is stiffer to handle, stretch, and set wrinkle-free, so the calculator adds labor hours as well as the higher material cost as you move up the mil presets. It is not simply the 20-mil price times a material multiplier.

    Does this check whether my pool's structure or bead track is sound?

    No. It prices the liner replacement scope you describe; it does not inspect the shell, verify the bead track or coping condition, or make a structural or code determination. Confirm the receiver track and wall condition in person before quoting a bead type or ordering vinyl.

vs-a-flat-2999-special.html.text:
← Vinyl Liner Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $2,999 special

"$2,999 for a 16×32" is a price for one water surface, quoted at a pool whose water surface can look almost the same while everything that actually costs money — the shape, the stairs, the liner, the track — is different.

What a flat water-surface special is

A flat special is the fastest way to quote: one headline number tied to one water-surface size, read off a postcard or a search result and repeated. Homeowners shop it because "16×32" is the easiest thing to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer will ask you to match at a pool that is a different shape entirely.

The number behind it was set for one pool — a rectangle, a hopper deep end, standard bead, no stairs, solid 20-mil vinyl — and then reused for every liner afterward keyed only to water surface, whether or not the next pool looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the shape, depth, mil, bead, stairs, pattern, and access, plus your loaded labor and overhead. It turns the geometry into liner square feet — wall vinyl, hopper extra, stair vinyl, and pattern waste, none of which show up in a water-surface figure — and returns a walk-away price for this pool, not a generic one.

What a flat special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Prices off water surface alone, so a 16×32 rectangle hopper (512 sq ft of water) and an 18×36 oval hopper with wedding-cake stairs and a patterned 27-mil liner (508.94 sq ft of water — almost identical) read as the same job. Prices the liner square feet the shape and stairs actually add, so this calculator's own numbers for the two jobs above are $5,319.79 and $9,946.51 — about 1.87× apart — even though their water surface barely differs.
Has no line for a new bead track, wedding-cake stairs, or a patterned liner's print-match waste — scope that changes labor and material without moving the water-surface number the rate is keyed to. Prices track, stairs, and pattern waste as their own line items, so a wedding-cake oval with a new track and a 27-mil pattern comes out priced differently from a plain rectangle at the same water surface.
Sets a "target margin" by marking cost up a flat percentage — cost × 1.25 for a "25% margin" — which is a markup on cost, not a share of price. Solves for the price that makes margin exactly the stated share of that price. On the $2,999-special job, a 25% markup on its $3,989.84 cost prices at $4,987.30 and actually clears only 20.0% margin; this calculator's $5,319.79 clears the full 25% the target asked for.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "labor rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the crew a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a homeowner asks to match the coupon price. Reports the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus the price per water square foot and per liner square foot, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied to a pool whose water surface looks the same but whose shape, stairs, and liner are not, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $2,999 special get the price wrong?

Because it is priced off water surface, and water surface is the one number that does not change much between an easy job and a hard one. A 16×32 rectangle hopper and an 18×36 oval hopper with wedding-cake stairs, a patterned 27-mil liner, and a new track have water surfaces of 512 and 508.94 square feet — practically identical — while this calculator's own price for the two jobs is $5,319.79 and $9,946.51, about 1.87× apart. The water-surface number cannot carry a difference it was never built to hold.

What does a flat special leave out that the water surface can't show?

The liner square feet, which is what is actually bought and installed. An oval's wall vinyl, hopper extra, stair vinyl, and pattern waste all add liner square feet without adding much water surface at all — the shape and the stairs eat the difference. A rate built around "square feet of water" has no line for any of that, so it prices two structurally different jobs the same.

Why does a new track or wedding-cake stairs matter if the pool looks the same size?

Because pool size, as most homeowners and even most flat rates mean it, is water surface — and a new bead track and wedding-cake stairs are both perimeter and labor items that scale with the shape and the steps, not with the water surface. Adding them to a job whose water surface has barely changed is exactly how a bid that looked like the last house comes in short.

What does solving margin as a share of price get right that a flat number misses?

A flat special, and most rough estimates built around one, price backward from a markup on cost — add 25% to what the job costs and call that the target margin. That is not the same number: margin is profit divided by price, not profit divided by cost, and a 25% markup on cost actually clears a lower margin than stated. This calculator solves for the price that hits the target margin exactly, so a target set at 25% comes out at 25%, not a smaller number wearing the same label.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, liner cost, or what a competitor's coupon charges. It takes the shape, depth, mil, bead, stairs, pattern, access, and your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat number skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat water-surface special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the next pool's shape stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business. This page is a free, private worksheet for one vinyl liner replacement before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes liner square feet, the hopper, the stairs, the bead, and the track, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a copyable customer-facing bid summary, and a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
